# Trichy assault rifle

The **Trichy assault rifle** (also known as **TAR**) is an Indian assault rifle chambered for the 7.62×39mm cartridge. It is manufactured by the Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT), a unit of Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited (AWEIL) . The rifle is a derivative of the Bulgarian Arsenal AR-M1, which itself is a variant of the Kalashnikov AK-47 pattern .

Designed to meet the operational requirements of Indian security forces engaged in counter-insurgency and law enforcement duties, the TAR was developed to provide a domestic alternative to imported AK-pattern rifles . Following its introduction in 2017, the weapon has been adopted by various Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF), including the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) and Border Security Force (BSF), as well as several state police units across India .

## History

### Background
Prior to the development of the Trichy assault rifle, Indian paramilitary and police forces relied heavily on a mix of weaponry, including the 5.56mm INSAS rifle and imported 7.62×39mm rifles such as the AK-47 and the Bulgarian Arsenal AR-M1 . While the Indian Army had standardized on the 5.56mm caliber for a period, operational experience in counter-insurgency environments led to a renewed preference for the stopping power of the 7.62×39mm cartridge among police and paramilitary units . To reduce dependence on imports and promote self-reliance in defense production, the Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli initiated the development of an indigenous platform compatible with the widely available 7.62×39mm ammunition .

### Development
The Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) began the development of the rifle around 2011 . Early prototypes reportedly utilized receivers based on the FN FAL design but adapted for the 7.62×39mm cartridge; however, the design eventually shifted toward a Kalashnikov-pattern mechanism based on the Bulgarian AR-M1 . Development continued between 2011 and 2015, with the establishment of a production line in 2017 .

Initial versions faced scrutiny regarding their rate of fire and reliability. Reports from 2012 indicated that prototypes experienced jamming issues attributed to a high rate of fire (800 rounds per minute), which exceeded the standard cyclic rate of the AK-47 . Subsequent refinements involved adjusting the mechanism to stabilize the rate of fire and improving the receiver construction .

### Trials and Adoption
The TAR underwent extensive field trials to validate its suitability for service. In November 2017, the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) conducted reliability tests at their academy in Kadarpur, Haryana . During these trials, the rifle was subjected to a life-cycle test involving the firing of 15,000 rounds without a reported stoppage . Additional environmental testing included exposure to mud, rain, and saltwater, as well as drop tests to assess durability .

Following successful trials, the CRPF placed an initial order for 6,167 rifles in early 2018 . The first batch of 500 rifles was handed over to the CRPF in March 2020 . The Chhattisgarh Police had previously acquired a batch of 200 rifles in March 2017 .

## Design

### Operating Mechanism
The Trichy assault rifle is a gas-operated firearm that utilizes a rotating bolt locking mechanism, consistent with the Kalashnikov pattern . It is capable of firing in single-shot, automatic, and burst modes . The weapon is chambered for the 7.62×39mm M43 cartridge, which is the same ammunition used by the AK-47 and AKM series .

### Receiver and Construction
A distinguishing feature of the TAR, compared to the stamped-receiver AKM or INSAS rifles, is its use of a fully machined mono-block receiver . This construction method is intended to provide higher strength and reliability, similar to the original AK-47 and the Bulgarian AR-M1 . The rifle features a fibre-reinforced polymer magazine with steel inserts and polymer furniture, including the handguard and pistol grip .

### Specifications
The standard TAR weighs approximately 3.4 kilograms (7.5 lb) without the magazine . It has an overall length of 900 millimeters (35 in) with the stock extended and 650 millimeters (26 in) with the stock folded . The barrel length is 414 mm (16.3 in) . The rifle has a cyclic rate of fire of approximately 600 to 650 rounds per minute . The effective firing range is stated to be between 300 and 350 meters, with a maximum destructive range cited as 1,350 meters .

### Features and Accessories
The TAR is designed with modularity in mind. It can be fitted with Picatinny rails on the upper handguard (12 o'clock position) to accommodate optical sights and other tactical accessories . The rifle is equipped with tritium-filled luminous sights for low-light operations . It is compatible with various under-barrel grenade launchers (UBGL), including the GP-25, GP-30, and Indian-manufactured 40mm UBGLs . The weapon feeds from a 30-round detachable box magazine and is compatible with standard AK-47 magazines .

## Variants

The Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli manufactures the TAR in several configurations to suit different operational requirements.

### Fixed Butt
The standard infantry version features a fixed buttstock, offering stability for general combat use .

### Side Folding Butt
This variant features a stock that folds to the side of the receiver. It was developed to reduce the overall length of the weapon for ease of transport and storage .

### Down Folding Butt
Launched in August 2021, this variant features an under-folding stock (down-folding). It was developed specifically to meet the requirements of the Railway Protection Force (RPF) and certain CAPF units for a more compact profile during guard and patrolling duties .

### Trichy Carbine (TriCa)
The **Trichy Carbine**, often abbreviated as **TriCa** or referred to as "Baby TAR," is a compact carbine version of the assault rifle unveiled in January 2021 . It features a shortened barrel of approximately 212 mm (8.3 in) and weighs 3.17 kg . The TriCa is designed for use by vehicle crews, paratroopers, and special operations forces requiring a concealable and maneuverable weapon . It has an effective range of 150 to 175 meters and features a special muzzle booster to mitigate flash and sound .

## Users

The Trichy assault rifle has been procured by various Indian security agencies.

* **Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF):** The CRPF placed a bulk order for 6,167 rifles following successful trials in 2017–2018 .
* **Border Security Force (BSF):** The BSF has inducted the TAR into service to replace older weaponry .
* **Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB):** Along with the BSF, the SSB has placed orders for the rifle .
* **Central Industrial Security Force (CISF):** The CISF is among the CAPF units that have procured the TAR .
* **National Security Guard (NSG):** The NSG placed an order for the TriCa carbine variant in December 2021 .
* **State Police Forces:**
 * **Chhattisgarh Police:** Received the first batch of 200 rifles in March 2017 for use in anti-Naxalite operations .
 * **Madhya Pradesh Police:** Procured the weapon for modernization .
 * **Rajasthan Police:** Identified as a user of the TAR .
 * **Kerala Police:** Inducted the TAR for counter-insurgency operations .
 * **Jharkhand Police:** Reported to have acquired the rifle for operations in left-wing extremism affected areas .
 * **Maharashtra Police:** Units such as the Mumbai Police have adopted the rifle .

6.content:
Ordnance Factory of Tiruchi (OFT) has developed a new 7.62x39mm assault rifle. From what can see, the Trichy Assault Rifle looks to be an improved version of India's 5.56mm INSAS rifle.

![Image 1: rifle tm tfb Trichy Assault Rifle photo](http://revolversinfo.blogspot.com/rifle-tm-tfb.jpg)

Times of India reports ...

> TIRUCHI: The Ordnance Factory of Tiruchi (OFT) has designed and developed an indigenous assault rifle matching the specifications of the AK47.
> 
> "When put into use by our armed forces and other security agencies, the rifle will be recognized as pride of India. It has been indigenously developed and has all the features of AK-47,'' said A K Prabhakar, OFT general manager, in an interaction with reporters on the sidelines of OFT Day celebrations. OFT, one among 41 such factories in the country, was established 45 years ago on the outskirts of the city.
> 
> To mark the contribution of the Tiruchi factory in developing the rifle, officials have decided to christen it "Trichy Assault Rifle,'' Prabhakar said. Field trials have been done for the 7.62mm caliber rifle with a range of 400 metres. "The rifle has been successfully tried by the Indian Army,'' Prabhakar said. It features a foldable butt and boasts of night vision device besides telescopic day vision system.

\[ Many thanks to Moa for emailing me the link. \]

If you were gonna go through the trouble of developing and adopting an entirely new rifle design, why would you base it around a 68 year old cartridge design? Has nobody in India heard of a Ballistic Coefficient? I can’t believe that the Chinese have already adopted a rifle that’s better than what India will be getting in the next decade.

The outer body looks completely like a FAL chambered in 7.62x39mm.

Looks like it takes a lot of inspiration from the FAL. $0.02

Well, it is’nt exactly an improved version of the INSAS by any means. It could be considered in theory a 7.62×39 equivalent of the Brazillian IMBEL MD-2. Instead of FAL parts as a base, the OFT clearly used components from the RFI SLR1A along with some FAL based components like the folding stock.

Like Matt said what a waste of effort and resources.

To be fair to the Indians, I think they have to consider the large stocks of 7.62×39 they have.

On the design – it looks like a FN FAL (or FNC) and AK47 had a love child!

I actually like it!

Not sure anyone could actually “Improve” the turd Insas.

Look Like FN CAL/IMBEL MD-97 in 7.62M43 with AK mag

FN CAL=> http://world.guns.ru/assault/be/fn-cal-e.html  
IMBEL MD-97=> http://world.guns.ru/assault/braz/imbel-md-97-e.html

Indian Armed Forces just needs to give up and buy a license from someone. The INSAS is routinely derided as horrible compromise of a design-by-committee rifle. The INSAS (and the Trichy here) are rather inflexible and it’s adherence to the Kalashnikov ergonomics and 7.62x39mm cartridge make them poor equivalents to modern 21st century assault rifles. I know they’re sticklers for reliability (Op. Meghdoot’s insane coldness had even their Kalashnikovs freezing up) but reliability for the expense of accuracy is just as bad as accuracy for the sake of reliability. It’s all the same if the round malfunctions the gun or misses wide in the end.

I hear Fabrique Nationale could use the money and the IA would probably love to be outfitted with SCARs or something.

“Why would you base it around a 68 year old cartridge design?” Several reasons:

1\. Logistics – you can gradually phase out the old rifles. Quite similar to the reason why the US is stuck with 5.56×45 and why all competing designs (6.5 Grendel, 6.8 SPC) tried to be as compatible as possible (same mags, same lower receiver…)

2\. Exports – if you want to sell a rifle to a different country, you make sure they can use up their old ammo. 7.62×39 is still one of the cheapest ammo choices there is, thanks to the former Soviet Union.

3\. It is not a bad bullet design for an assault rifle. Ballistic coefficient may not be good, but this is for India and not the US Army, which, all snide remarks aside, has an impressive marksmanship program(\*) that other countries can rarely measure up to.

4\. It works very well in the AK system – you do not have to recalculate measurements. Let’s not fall for marketing lingo here: “Indigenously developed” probably means “locally produced” and not “developed from scratch”.

(\*) The appropriate snide remark would be: How else could the US deal with having a great, but prissy sporting rifle as military rifle?

it looks more FAL based than AK based

The lower receiver geometry looks more FAL-like to me.

more than a INSAS derivate it seems to be a FN FAL/Rifle 7.62mm 1A1 (as it was called in india) with a INSAS gas block and berall profile, adapted to fire the m43 cartidge…

The AK is a prooven design, it’s probably going to be around for a very long time.

Why not just adopt the AKM or AK-103 then. The INAS has many problems I heard.

The reason I think they’re sticking with the 7.62x39mm is because their small-arms ammo production facilities are probably very oriented around producing this round. Add to that the fact that it’s cheap to produce, it makes little for them economically and logistically to switch to another round.

Also considering the probable training standards of the Indian military, I see little reason for them to switch to another round.

=========================================

Bulk orders for Indian-made AK-47s have stabilised the Atmanirbhar design plan, helping the Ordnance Factory Board innovate and create a compact version of the assault rifle

'Baby TAR', India’s smallest assault rifle

[![Image 4: Sandeep Unnithan](https://akm-img-a-in.tosshub.com/indiatoday/images/reporter/201901/image005_0-770x433-profile_image_one_to_one_1.jpg?VersionId=.pasKkvdD84ULmLha3vENVAV69BnJMOd&size=50:50)](https://www.indiatoday.in/author/sandeep-unnithan "Sandeep Unnithan")

[Sandeep Unnithan](https://www.indiatoday.in/author/sandeep-unnithan "Sandeep Unnithan")[](https://twitter.com/@SandeepUnnithan "Sandeep Unnithan")

Delhi,UPDATED: Jan 25, 2021 20:23 IST

![Image 5](https://akm-img-a-in.tosshub.com/indiatoday/images/mediamanager/india_today_insight.jpg?IzvocAu7gyMv.UA3nBmTl5xRnm990vx3)It’s laptop-sized, can be carried inside a coat and can spit AK-47 bullets out at the rate of roughly 700 rounds per minute. Meet the ‘Baby TAR’, India’s smallest assault rifle. Developed by the Indian Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappali, the weapon is a compact version of the legendary AK-47, which the factory has been mass-producing since 2017. This in-house OFB innovation comes soon after the Indian Army unveiled a 9x19mm carbine developed in-house.

advertisement

The TAR-3, a compact, fully automatic version of the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), recently passed a series of trials at the Ordnance Factory Trichy (OF Trichy). A dozen prototypes have been produced during the lockdown. The weapon is currently undergoing ‘unofficial trials’ with the Indian Army, where three prototypes are believed to have fired over 2,000 rounds each without stoppages.

The ‘Baby TAR’ fires the same 7.62x39 mm cartridge as the AK-47—this ammunition is in widespread production and use, thereby easing logistics. It uses the AK-47’s distinctive 30-round curved box magazine and features a commonality of parts with existing weapons. Its designers chopped down the AK-47’s 16-inch barrel, producing a weapon with an 8.3-inch barrel and an effective range of 150 metres. The TAR-3 is 19.2 inches long with its stock folded, and at 2.7 kg (unloaded), is one kg lighter than the AK-47. It has a monoblock receiver, shockproof polymer lower parts and two Picatinny rails that can mount a variety of sights and scopes.

ALSO READ | [The Indian Army’s ‘General Kalashnikov’ gives it a new 9 mm sub-machine gun](https://www.indiatoday.in/india-today-insight/story/the-indian-army-s-general-kalashnikov-gives-it-a-new-9-mm-sub-machine-gun-1759202-2021-01-14)

Its designers say it is ideal for users like special forces and counter-terrorist operators who want compact, concealable weapons but with the firepower of a full-sized AK-47. The assault rifle is also suitable for aircraft, tank and vehicle crews. Significantly, the weapon was developed as an unsolicited design—without waiting for army General Staff Qualitative Requirements (GSQRs), which usually is the start point for weapon development. To do so, the factory used the experience it gained from mass producing the Trichy Assault Rifle, a wholly indigenous copy of the AK-47.

Designers at OF Trichy appear to have solved a problem that stumped the gun designers of the DRDO’s now-discarded INSAS carbine variant in the 1990s—how to reduce the barrel heating and the excessive sound and flash produced when an assault rifle bullet is fired from a short barrel. The DRDO did it by switching over to a smaller bullet, the 5.56x30 round used in the JVPC carbine. The Baby TAR designers solved the problem by used internal metal reflectors to insulate the foregrip from the barrel and by designing, in-house, a compact flash hider at the barrel muzzle. The gun can presently fire four full magazines—around 120 rounds—without the barrel heating. This development is noteworthy because it means Indian designers now understand the ‘know-why’, rather than just the ‘know-how’ that they would have gained from a licensed production.

advertisement

**Compacting the AK**

The Soviet Union began producing compact, stubbier versions of its AK-74 rifle (an AK-47 evolution firing the 5.45x39 mm cartridge) in the 1970s. Copies of this compact assault rifle have been famously attached to Osama bin Laden, ISIS chief Abu Bakr Al Baghdadi and more recently, Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko. Compact versions of the AK-47 believed to have been produced in the frontier regions of Pakistan, have been recovered by Indian security forces from terrorists in Jammu and Kashmir in recent months.

Trichy is one of two Indian ordnance factories already mass-producing Indian versions of the legendary Kalashnikov (the original weapon was never patented and is freely made by countries across the world). The ‘Ghatak’, a copy made by Rifle Factory Ishapore, did not find as much favour. The full-sized TAR is believed to be a copy of the Bulgarian AR-M1, itself a licensed copy of the Kalashnikov. Over 500,000 Bulgarian weapons have been imported by India’s central, state and paramilitary forces over the past decade—the TAR, which began bulk production in 2017, has also helped reducing imports from that east European country. OF Trichy has developed four variants of the rifle, with fixed, side-folding, under-folding and telescoping butts. Nearly 20,000 weapons have been delivered to the Indian police, paramilitary and central armed police forces. Interestingly, each TAR costs around Rs 55,000—far less than the licensed AK-203 to be produced by Indo-Russian Rifles, which will cost upwards of Rs 75,000. And the compact version could cost less than the full-length TAR.

advertisement

The compact TAR’s arrival has added to growing numbers of indigenously designed small arms. From a virtual drought a few years back, there are now multiple indigenous designs available, chambered for various cartridges. Besides the Army’s 9x19mm carbine, the DRDO has developed a variant firing a 5.56x45 mm cartridge, for a different Army requirement. The JVPC, a DRDO-OFB carbine, passed Army and MHA development trials last year. Bengaluru-based small arms start up SSS Defence has its own designs for weapons, chambered for 5.56x45 and 7.62x39 cartridges, and an upgrade kit for existing AK-47 variants. All these designs, of course, are at the prototype stage and will need to fire several thousand rounds before they are fit for mass-production and induction.

Trichy factory churns out desi 'AK-47' rifles

The Ordnance Factory Trichy (OFT) has dispatched 200 indigenously developed assault rifles to Chhattisgarh police.

![Image 2: Trichy factory churns out desi 'AK-47' rifles](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-57713628,imgsize-33820,width-400,height-225,resizemode-72/57713628.jpg)

The rifles have a range of 500 metres, on par with AK-47 rifles. (Photo: R Baskar).

TRICHY: The Ordnance Factory Trichy (OFT) has dispatched 200 indigenously developed assault rifles to Chhattisgarh police.  
K Appa Rao, general manager, OFT, handed over the 7.62x 39mm rifles, which have a range of 500 meters, at par with AK-47 rifles, to Ratan Lal Dangi, DIG, Chattisgarh, during the 216th Ordnance Factory Day held here on Saturday.

![Image 3: 1x1 polls](https://static.toiimg.com/photo/25581306.cms)

  
The assault rifle uses 7.62x39mm ammunition made by ordnance factories in Varangoan and Bhusawal. It can be fired in single shot, automatic and burst fire mode. In automatic mode, the weapon fires 600 rounds per minute, in short series, at a group or single targets at a distance upto 500 metres. However, it is most effective at a distance upto 300 metres, officials said.  
The design of the model permits attaching a 40mm Under Barrel Grenade Launcher (UBGL) and 40X46mm Under Barrel Grenade Launcher (UBGL-M6), they added.  
K Appa Rao said central armed paramilitary forces like CRPF, BSF and certain elite forces of the Army, such as Rashtriya Rifles and [Assam](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/topic/assam) Rifles were using imported AK-47 rifles in counter insurgency operations and extremist violence.

TIRUCHY: Ordnance Factory Tiruchy (OFT) on Thursday handed over the first consignment of 500 assault rifles to CRPF. Trichy Assault Rifles or TAR, as these are called, are the indigenous version of AK-47 rifle. Shirish Khare, GM, OFT  handed over the rifles to DS Rawat, DIG, CRPF. OFT started development of the rifle in 2015, and established a production line in 2017. The first batch of 200 TARs was delivered to Chandigarh police in March 2017. In November 2017, the CRPF tested the rifle for functionality and reliability. It was subjected to a life cycle test by firing 15,000 rounds in one go.

In February 2018, the TAR was deployed for field trial at Jagdalpur, Raipur, Guwahati and Srinagar. Following this, order for 6167 rifles were placed.OFT would supply TARs in both fixed and foldable butt models, sources said adding that the latter was in the development stage. The TAR is compatible with GP-25, 30 and UBGL M-6 grenade launchers.

OFT has so far supplied more than 10,000 rifles to Central Armed Police Forces including the BSF, SSB, ITBP & CISF. Police force in several States have also inducted TAR under their modernisation scheme.   
OFT has also taken up research and development projects such as the trial of 7.62X39mm TAR Carbine(long barrel firearm) and 40X46mm UBGL (Underbarrel Grenade Launcher) for TAR/AK 47, which after induction would serve as an import substitute.

The **Trichy assault rifle** (TAR), sometimes known as the **Tiruchi assault rifle**,[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3) is an [Indian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India")\-made [assault rifle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assault_rifle "Assault rifle") chambered for the [7.62×39mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7.62%C3%9739mm "7.62×39mm") round. The TAR is based on the [AR-M1](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AR-M1 "AR-M1"), produced by [Bulgarian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulgaria "Bulgaria") manufacturer [Arsenal AD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsenal_AD "Arsenal AD"). Developed between 2011 and 2015, [Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ordnance_Factory_Tiruchirappalli "Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli") (OFT) began manufacturing TARs in 2017.

The TAR was developed to reduce dependence on [imported](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Import "Import") AR-M1s under the [Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmanirbhar_Bharat "Atmanirbhar Bharat") self-reliance policy. The TAR has been adopted by most [Indian law enforcement agencies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law_enforcement_in_India "Law enforcement in India").

Prior to the TAR's introduction, India largely used foreign-made [AK-style](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kalashnikov_rifle "Kalashnikov rifle") rifles. Around 500,000 M1s were reportedly imported by India from Bulgaria in 2021 for use by the [Central Armed Police Forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Armed_Police_Forces "Central Armed Police Forces") (CAPF) and [Indian police forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Police_Service "Indian Police Service").[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4) As of May 2025, India is the [second-largest arms importer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arms_industry#World's_largest_arms_importers "Arms industry") after [Ukraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ukraine "Ukraine"), accounting for 8.3% of the arms trade, according to research data from the [Stockholm International Peace Research Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stockholm_International_Peace_Research_Institute "Stockholm International Peace Research Institute").[\[5\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-5) To reduce dependence on importing small arms from other countries, part of the [Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atmanirbhar_Bharat "Atmanirbhar Bharat") policy called for self-sufficiency to manufacture firearms in India.[\[6\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-6)

OFT announced the manufacture of an indigenous AK-based assault rifle in 2011.[\[7\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-oldnew-8) The AR was named Trichy after OFT to recognise the factory's contribution in developing and manufacturing the rifle.[\[9\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-9) Some TARs were made in 2012 to be tested.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10) These early TARs were tested by the [Border Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Border_Security_Force "Border Security Force") (BSF), the [Central Reserve Police Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Reserve_Police_Force "Central Reserve Police Force") (CRPF), the [Indo-Tibetan Border Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indo-Tibetan_Border_Police "Indo-Tibetan Border Police") and the [Sashastra Seema Bal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sashastra_Seema_Bal "Sashastra Seema Bal").[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10)

Development started in 2015[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11) with a production line established in 2017.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12)[\[13\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-13) That March, 200 TARs were acquired by the [Chhattisgarh Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chhattisgarh_Police "Chhattisgarh Police")[\[14\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TrichyF-14) as part of the 216th Ordnance Factories Day celebration.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15) Concerns were raised at the time, prior to manufacture, that OFT was experiencing manpower decline, leading to a decline of employees at the company.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THA-16) The [All India Defence Employees Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All_India_Defence_Employees_Federation "All India Defence Employees Federation"), the [Indian National Defence Workers' Federation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_National_Defence_Workers%27_Federation "Indian National Defence Workers' Federation"), and the [Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bharatiya_Pratiraksha_Mazdoor_Sangh "Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh") stated their opposition to importing small arms with the unions hoping that more orders for the TAR would be approved, retaining employees at OFT.[\[16\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THA-16)

[![Image 3](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg/250px-Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg)

A [CISF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force") officer practices with the TAR at a shooting range.

In November 2017, the CRPF conducted field tests to determine the suitability of the TAR with 15,000 rounds fired[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12) at the [CRPF Academy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CRPF_Academy "CRPF Academy") in Kadarpur, [Haryana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haryana "Haryana") with no reports of the rifle jamming.[\[17\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-17) Other tests conducted included the TAR being fired from mud, rain and saltwater and from being dropped to test reliability and accuracy.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) 100 TARs were ordered afterwards.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) In February 2018, further tests were conducted by the CRPF at Jagdalpur, Raipur, Guwahati and Srinagar with an order of 6,167 TARs placed afterwards.[\[12\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12) At the time, the CRPF tested the Trichy with the Ghatak, the [Joint Venture Protective Carbine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Venture_Protective_Carbine "Joint Venture Protective Carbine") and the [INSAS](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/INSAS_rifle "INSAS rifle")1C.[\[19\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-19) In March 2020, the CRPF acquired the first 500 out of 6,167 TARs sold to them.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11)

In January 2019, the TAR was delivered to the BSF, with its Additional Director General Nasir Kamal receiving the first rifle from the [Ordnance Factory Board](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Directorate_of_Ordnance_/(Coordination_%26_Services/) "Directorate of Ordnance (Coordination & Services)")'s Director General Saurabh Kumar.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3) It was reported in the same month that the [Jharkhand Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jharkhand_Police "Jharkhand Police") would acquire TARs for anti-Naxalite operations.[\[20\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-JPR-20) The TAR was displayed for the first time at the Pragati Maidan in [New Delhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi "New Delhi") for the 5th International Police Expo and the 4th India Homeland Security Expo.[\[21\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-21) In February 2020, the TAR was on public display at the Defence Expo at [Lucknow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucknow "Lucknow"), [Uttar Pradesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22) It was reported at the time that the TAR was offered to the [Indian Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_Army "Indian Army").[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22) OFT reported in March 2021 that around 11,500 TARs were supplied for a total of [Rs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rupee_sign "Rupee sign") 1.60 billion during fiscal year 2020–21.[\[23\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-23)

In January 2021, the TriCa (Trichy Carbine) Carbine was unveiled.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) Tests were conducted where 2,000 rounds were fired with no stoppages.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4) That August, OFT announced that the TAR could use the [ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARDE_Under_Barrel_Grenade_Launcher "ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher"), which was presented by OFT general manager Sanjay Dwivedi.[\[24\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-UBGL-24) A TAR variant with a downfolding stock was presented publicly.[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-PR-25) This variant was sought out by the [Railway Protection Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Railway_Protection_Force "Railway Protection Force") aside from the CAPFs.[\[26\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-26) In December 2021, the [National Security Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") placed an order of 100 TriCa carbines.[\[27\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NSGTriCa-27) On April 2022, the [Kerala Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_Police "Kerala Police") (KP) ordered 92 TriCa carbines.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPTriCa-28) According to OFT, the [Greyhounds unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greyhounds_/(police/) "Greyhounds (police)") ordered 44 TARs.[\[28\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPTriCa-28) In July 2022, the [Government of Kerala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Kerala "Government of Kerala") received a request from KP to procure 250 TARs with side folding stocks;[\[29\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-29) they received the TriCa carbines in May 2025.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPH-30) According to the [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India "Advanced Weapons and Equipment India")'s (AWEIL) 2022–2023 Annual Report, the [National Security Guard](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") and the [Andhra Pradesh Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Andhra_Pradesh_Police "Andhra Pradesh Police") conducted tests on both the TAR and the TriCa carbine.[\[31\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-31)

In January 2023, the [Central Industrial Security Force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force") (CISF) received TARs manufactured from [Rifle Factory Ishapore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rifle_Factory_Ishapore "Rifle Factory Ishapore").[\[32\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-32) That April, Minister of State for Defence and Tourism [Ajay Bhatt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ajay_Bhatt_/(politician/) "Ajay Bhatt (politician)") visited OFT, where he witnessed the TAR being manufactured in the factory while briefed on OFT's research and development work.[\[33\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-33) The following January, BSF procured further TARs featuring bayonets.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Bayonet-34) The Government of Kerala published an approved plan for the KP to acquire 30 TARs.[\[35\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-35) In November 2023, the Trichy was on display at the Dasara Exhibition in [Mysore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mysore "Mysore"), [Karnataka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnataka "Karnataka") as part of an effort to raise awareness on crime and public safety.[\[36\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-36) In a July 2024 interview with Rajesh Choudhary, Chairman and Managing Director of AWEIL, he said that the TAR continues to be in demand with CAPFs and reported that an export order was made for the rifle.[\[37\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-AWEILI-37) In May 2025, it was reported that the Assam Forest Department and the [Central Bureau of Narcotics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Bureau_of_Narcotics "Central Bureau of Narcotics") made orders for the TriCa carbine.[\[30\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPH-30)

Initial versions of the TAR were produced by using [FN FAL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FN_FAL "FN FAL")\-based receivers and were using 7.62x39 mm magazines.[\[8\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-oldnew-8) In 2012, there were reports that the prototypes jammed during testing due to the rate of fire being 800 rounds per minutes instead of 600 rounds per minute to match with the AK-47.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10) It was initially expected that the rate of fire would be at 650 rounds per minute.[\[10\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10)

The current version of the TAR is based on the AR-M1[\[38\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-38) with a machined receiver instead of stamped sheet to ensure the rifle has high accuracy and reliability.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) The TAR can be outfitted with [picatinny rails](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Picatinny_rail "Picatinny rail") on the upper handguard to attach scopes if requested.[\[18\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18)

In July 2021, it was reported that the TARs used by the [Kerala Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kerala_Police "Kerala Police") are effective in [Naxalite-Maoist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Naxalite%E2%80%93Maoist_insurgency "Naxalite–Maoist insurgency") [counterinsurgency operations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterinsurgency "Counterinsurgency").[\[39\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-39)

On August 2025, a TAR was secured from pro-Maoist communist [Naxalite fighters](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People%27s_Liberation_Guerrilla_Army_/(India/) "People's Liberation Guerrilla Army (India)") in Chhattisgarh’s [Narayanpur district](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narayanpur_district "Narayanpur district").[\[40\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-cp-40)

The TAR can fire with single, burst and full automatic mode.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)[\[41\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TrichyDemand-41) OFT reported that the TAR can be adopted with single shot mode only for police forces in cities and urban areas.[\[1\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-OFTTR-1) While it has an effective range of 300 to 350 metres,[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)[\[42\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-AWEIL2122-42) the range can be up to 500 metres if the rifle is used in full auto.[\[15\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15)

OFT claimed that the TAR is functionally on par with the AK-47.[\[22\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22)

The TAR can be equipped with several [underbarrel grenade launchers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grenade_launcher "Grenade launcher"), including the [ARDE UBGL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ARDE_Under_Barrel_Grenade_Launcher "ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher"),[\[43\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-43) the [GP-25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GP-25 "GP-25"), the GP-30 and the Arsenal M6 UBGL.[\[11\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11) The TAR can use bayonets.[\[34\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Bayonet-34)

[Magazines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magazine_/(firearms/) "Magazine (firearms)") for the TAR are supplied by Nilkamal Limited.[\[44\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-44) Magazines made for [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47")\-based assault rifles can also be used.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-na-45)

[7.62×39 mm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/7.62%C3%9739_mm "7.62×39 mm") ammunition of all types can be used for the TAR.[\[45\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-na-45)

### Trichy assault rifle

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=11 "Edit section: Trichy assault rifle")\]

Main variant with a fixed stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)

### Trichy folding stock (side)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Trichy folding stock (side)")\]

TAR variant with a side folding stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)

### Trichy folding stock (down)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: Trichy folding stock (down)")\]

Unveiled on August 2021, it is a TAR variant with a downfolding stock.[\[3\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3)[\[25\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-PR-25)

It's sometimes referred to as a variant with an underfolding stock.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4)

### Trichy Carbine (TriCa)

\[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Trichy_assault_rifle&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Trichy Carbine (TriCa)")\]

Unveiled on January 2021, the TriCa weights 3.17 kg and is marketed as a compact weapon for vehicle crews, paratroopers and special forces units.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) The TriCA's firing range is from 150-175 metres.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) A muzzle device is installed on the barrel to minimize muzzle flash and sound when it's fired.[\[2\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2)

The TriCa is a clone based on the Arsenal AR-M14SF, but the muzzle device is based on the AKS-74U.[\[a\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-47)[\[46\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-MILMAG-46)

It is sometimes known as **Baby TAR** or **TAR-3**.[\[4\]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4)

Indian 7.62x39mm FAL
====================

The Indian government manufacturer [Ordnance Factories Board](http://ofbindia.gov.in/index.php) (OFB) displayed a FAL based rifle chambered in 7.62x39mm. The TRICHY Assault Rifle (TAR) is designed to utilize the Indian A7 cartridge, a locally produced 7.62x39mm. The internal operation retains the piston system and is the tilting bolt design found in the FAL. I am unaware if it has the same gas adjustment capabilities.

[![Image 2: Trichy 7.62x39mm FAL](http://aftermathgunclub.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/Trichy-7.62x39mm-FAL.jpg)](http://aftermathgunclub.com/wp-content/uploads/2014/02/Trichy-7.62x39mm-FAL.jpg)  
The weapon was designed to be modular and reduced in weight. Some key features include a perforated flash hider, FN style folding stock, an optic mount, polymer handguards, and polymer pistol grip. The TRICHY rifle can also be equipped with a grenade launcher.

The rifle is 37″ long (940 mm) and 27.16″ with the stock folded (690 mm), with a weight of 7.9 lbs (3.6 kg). Rate of fire is 800 rounds per minute from a 30 round magazine – this is a faster rate of fire than the AKM (600 r/m) or the FAL (600-700 r/m). I suspected this increase of rate of fire would be problematic for the shooter, and I quickly found an article on it in the [Times Of India](http://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/nagpur/Indian-AK-47-too-fast-for-its-own-good/articleshow/11482089.cms?referral=PM).

        I don’t think you’ll be able to procure any kit of this rifle. The Trichy Assault Rifle shown over here is one of the two prototypes of Trichy Assault Rifle developed by OFB. During the developmental phase of TAR the OFB developed two prototypes.
        
        One was based on the FN FAL, it even used the tilting breechblock operation of FN FAL. Other prototype was based on the Bulgarian AR-M1 milled receiver AK.
        
        Although both of them passed the initial trials the Indian govt. opted for the AR-M1 based prototype because the FN FAL based prototype didn’t meet the budget constraints specified by the Indian govt.

14.content:
### Background

Prior to the TAR's introduction, India largely used foreign-made [AK-style](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Kalashnikov_rifle "Kalashnikov rifle") rifles. Around 500,000 M1s were reportedly imported by India from Bulgaria in 2021 for use by the [Central Armed Police Forces](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Central_Armed_Police_Forces "Central Armed Police Forces") (CAPF) and [Indian police forces](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Indian_Police_Service "Indian Police Service").[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4) As of May 2025, India is the [second-largest arms importer](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Arms_industry#World's_largest_arms_importers "Arms industry") after [Ukraine](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ukraine "Ukraine"), accounting for 8.3% of the arms trade, according to research data from the [Stockholm International Peace Research Institute](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Stockholm_International_Peace_Research_Institute "Stockholm International Peace Research Institute").[\[5\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-5) To reduce dependence on importing small arms from other countries, part of the [Atmanirbhar Bharat](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Atmanirbhar_Bharat "Atmanirbhar Bharat") policy called for self-sufficiency to manufacture firearms in India.[\[6\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-6)

OFT announced the manufacture of an indigenous AK-based assault rifle in 2011.[\[7\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-7)[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-oldnew-8) The AR was named Trichy after OFT to recognise the factory's contribution in developing and manufacturing the rifle.[\[9\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-9) Some TARs were made in 2012 to be tested.[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10) These early TARs were tested by the [Border Security Force](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Border_Security_Force "Border Security Force") (BSF), the [Central Reserve Police Force](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Central_Reserve_Police_Force "Central Reserve Police Force") (CRPF), the [Indo-Tibetan Border Police](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Indo-Tibetan_Border_Police "Indo-Tibetan Border Police") and the [Sashastra Seema Bal](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Sashastra_Seema_Bal "Sashastra Seema Bal").[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10)

Development started in 2015[\[11\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11) with a production line established in 2017.[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12)[\[13\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-13) That March, 200 TARs were acquired by the [Chhattisgarh Police](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Chhattisgarh_Police "Chhattisgarh Police")[\[14\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TrichyF-14) as part of the 216th Ordnance Factories Day celebration.[\[15\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THOF-15) Concerns were raised at the time, prior to manufacture, that OFT was experiencing manpower decline, leading to a decline of employees at the company.[\[16\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THA-16) The [All India Defence Employees Federation](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/All_India_Defence_Employees_Federation "All India Defence Employees Federation"), the [Indian National Defence Workers' Federation](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Indian_National_Defence_Workers'_Federation "Indian National Defence Workers' Federation"), and the [Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Bharatiya_Pratiraksha_Mazdoor_Sangh "Bharatiya Pratiraksha Mazdoor Sangh") stated their opposition to importing small arms with the unions hoping that more orders for the TAR would be approved, retaining employees at OFT.[\[16\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THA-16)

### Adoption

[![Image 1: Thumb](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg/640px-Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg)](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#/media/File:Firing_TAR_at_range.jpg)

A [CISF](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force") officer practices with the TAR at a shooting range.

In November 2017, the CRPF conducted field tests to determine the suitability of the TAR with 15,000 rounds fired[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12) at the [CRPF Academy](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/CRPF_Academy "CRPF Academy") in Kadarpur, [Haryana](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Haryana "Haryana") with no reports of the rifle jamming.[\[17\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-17) Other tests conducted included the TAR being fired from mud, rain and saltwater and from being dropped to test reliability and accuracy.[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) 100 TARs were ordered afterwards.[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) In February 2018, further tests were conducted by the CRPF at Jagdalpur, Raipur, Guwahati and Srinagar with an order of 6,167 TARs placed afterwards.[\[12\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NIETAR-12) At the time, the CRPF tested the Trichy with the Ghatak, the [Joint Venture Protective Carbine](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Joint_Venture_Protective_Carbine "Joint Venture Protective Carbine") and the [INSAS](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/INSAS_rifle "INSAS rifle")1C.[\[19\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-19) In March 2020, the CRPF acquired the first 500 out of 6,167 TARs sold to them.[\[11\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-THTAR-11)

In January 2019, the TAR was delivered to the BSF, with its Additional Director General Nasir Kamal receiving the first rifle from the [Ordnance Factory Board](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Directorate_of_Ordnance_/(Coordination_&_Services/) "Directorate of Ordnance (Coordination & Services)")'s Director General Saurabh Kumar.[\[3\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-HinduBSF-3) It was reported in the same month that the [Jharkhand Police](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Jharkhand_Police "Jharkhand Police") would acquire TARs for anti-Naxalite operations.[\[20\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-JPR-20) The TAR was displayed for the first time at the Pragati Maidan in [New Delhi](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/New_Delhi "New Delhi") for the 5th International Police Expo and the 4th India Homeland Security Expo.[\[21\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-21) In February 2020, the TAR was on public display at the Defence Expo at [Lucknow](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Lucknow "Lucknow"), [Uttar Pradesh](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Uttar_Pradesh "Uttar Pradesh").[\[22\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22) It was reported at the time that the TAR was offered to the [Indian Army](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Indian_Army "Indian Army").[\[22\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-DFTAR-22) OFT reported in March 2021 that around 11,500 TARs were supplied for a total of [Rs](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Rupee_sign "Rupee sign") 1.60 billion during fiscal year 2020–21.[\[23\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-23)

In January 2021, the TriCa (Trichy Carbine) Carbine was unveiled.[\[2\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-TITR-2) Tests were conducted where 2,000 rounds were fired with no stoppages.[\[4\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-BT-4) That August, OFT announced that the TAR could use the [ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/ARDE_Under_Barrel_Grenade_Launcher "ARDE Under Barrel Grenade Launcher"), which was presented by OFT general manager Sanjay Dwivedi.[\[24\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-UBGL-24) A TAR variant with a downfolding stock was presented publicly.[\[25\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-PR-25) This variant was sought out by the [Railway Protection Force](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Railway_Protection_Force "Railway Protection Force") aside from the CAPFs.[\[26\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-26) In December 2021, the [National Security Guard](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") placed an order of 100 TriCa carbines.[\[27\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-NSGTriCa-27) On April 2022, the [Kerala Police](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Kerala_Police "Kerala Police") (KP) ordered 92 TriCa carbines.[\[28\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPTriCa-28) According to OFT, the [Greyhounds unit](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Greyhounds_/(police/) "Greyhounds (police)") ordered 44 TARs.[\[28\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPTriCa-28) In July 2022, the [Government of Kerala](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Government_of_Kerala "Government of Kerala") received a request from KP to procure 250 TARs with side folding stocks;[\[29\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-29) they received the TriCa carbines in May 2025.[\[30\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPH-30) According to the [Advanced Weapons and Equipment India](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Advanced_Weapons_and_Equipment_India "Advanced Weapons and Equipment India")'s (AWEIL) 2022–2023 Annual Report, the [National Security Guard](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/National_Security_Guard "National Security Guard") and the [Andhra Pradesh Police](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Andhra_Pradesh_Police "Andhra Pradesh Police") conducted tests on both the TAR and the TriCa carbine.[\[31\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-31)

In January 2023, the [Central Industrial Security Force](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Central_Industrial_Security_Force "Central Industrial Security Force") (CISF) received TARs manufactured from [Rifle Factory Ishapore](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Rifle_Factory_Ishapore "Rifle Factory Ishapore").[\[32\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-32) That April, Minister of State for Defence and Tourism [Ajay Bhatt](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Ajay_Bhatt_/(politician/) "Ajay Bhatt (politician)") visited OFT, where he witnessed the TAR being manufactured in the factory while briefed on OFT's research and development work.[\[33\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-33) The following January, BSF procured further TARs featuring bayonets.[\[34\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Bayonet-34) The Government of Kerala published an approved plan for the KP to acquire 30 TARs.[\[35\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-35) In November 2023, the Trichy was on display at the Dasara Exhibition in [Mysore](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Mysore "Mysore"), [Karnataka](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Karnataka "Karnataka") as part of an effort to raise awareness on crime and public safety.[\[36\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-36) In a July 2024 interview with Rajesh Choudhary, Chairman and Managing Director of AWEIL, he said that the TAR continues to be in demand with CAPFs and reported that an export order was made for the rifle.[\[37\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-AWEILI-37) In May 2025, it was reported that the Assam Forest Department and the [Central Bureau of Narcotics](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Central_Bureau_of_Narcotics "Central Bureau of Narcotics") made orders for the TriCa carbine.[\[30\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-KPH-30)

### Development

Initial versions of the TAR were produced by using [FN FAL](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/FN_FAL "FN FAL")\-based receivers and were using 7.62x39 mm magazines.[\[8\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-oldnew-8) In 2012, there were reports that the prototypes jammed during testing due to the rate of fire being 800 rounds per minutes instead of 600 rounds per minute to match with the AK-47.[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10) It was initially expected that the rate of fire would be at 650 rounds per minute.[\[10\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-Test-10)

The current version of the TAR is based on the AR-M1[\[38\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-38) with a machined receiver instead of stamped sheet to ensure the rifle has high accuracy and reliability.[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18) The TAR can be outfitted with [picatinny rails](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Picatinny_rail "Picatinny rail") on the upper handguard to attach scopes if requested.[\[18\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-CRPFTRCY-18)

### Combat use

In July 2021, it was reported that the TARs used by the [Kerala Police](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Kerala_Police "Kerala Police") are effective in [Naxalite-Maoist](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Naxalite%E2%80%93Maoist_insurgency "Naxalite–Maoist insurgency") [counterinsurgency operations](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Counterinsurgency "Counterinsurgency").[\[39\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-39)

On August 2025, a TAR was secured from pro-Maoist communist [Naxalite fighters](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/People's_Liberation_Guerrilla_Army_/(India/) "People's Liberation Guerrilla Army (India)") in Chhattisgarh’s [Narayanpur district](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Narayanpur_district "Narayanpur district").[\[40\]](https://www.wikiwand.com/en/articles/Trichy_assault_rifle#cite_note-cp-40)

BSF To Procure More Made-In-India Trichy Assault Rifles
=======================================================

BSF To Procure More Made-In-India Trichy Assault Rifles

Monday, January 15, 2024 by [Indian Defence News](https://www.blogger.com/profile/10039798451461108617)


==================================================================================================================================================================

![Image 2](https://blogger.googleusercontent.com/img/b/R29vZ2xl/AVvXsEjR_6KQW-dlRmJMFDgkmJHvIN6zxHHRz5SCWtwdpwIofRbn7S_6-PzX_cjkFy-Avno7sfNWct0lxVm8lRexBNOb7fRJVXpxtsvP6LGQI0GJPlA9ZiXQ25gYOts4kOHXAZ8rhyJ8xPms7zLIbNnKoaPVR_ApisaikLnKsTCB_20EZB-yBvfvin85iwJrk1E/s16000/Trichy_Assault_Rifle.jpg)

  

_BSF plans to arm its personnel with the 125 more indigenous Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), with bayonets and accessories in a limited procurement_

  

**New Delhi:** The Border Security Force (BSF) is gearing up to equip its personnel with the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), an indigenously developed firearm, according to an official statement. The procurement is set at a limited quantity, with the BSF acquiring 125 rifles along with bayonets and other accessory items.

  

TAR: Firepower Tailored For Specialised Needs of Paramilitary

  

The primary objective behind this move is to set an example for other wings of the Armed Forces and Paramilitary, encouraging them to follow suit and procure more indigenous arms. The initiative aims to strengthen India's self-sufficiency in defence capabilities.

  

“Ordnance Factory, Trichirappalli developed and manufactured TAR Down folding butt version to meet the customer requirement as some of the CAPF units, State Police and RPF required the Down folding butt version for quick and easy movement of personnel in guard and patrolling duty”, said Officials in a prior statement.

  

Trichy Assault Rifle: Counter-Terror Operations with Cutting-Edge Firepower

  

> _1\. The TAR, chambered in 7.62x39mm, has a lightweight modular design, making it well-suited for counter-insurgency and counter-terror operations._
> 
> _2\. Its gas-operated mechanism, machined mono-block receiver body, and fibre-reinforced polymer magazine with steel inserts contribute to its effectiveness in the field._
> 
> _3\. The rifle operates in both single-shot and burst modes, with the latter capable of destroying targets at a range of up to 500m. The TAR's overall destructive range extends to 1350m._
> 
> _4\. A customised version featuring a single-round firing mode is designed specifically for police forces engaged in patrolling duties within urban areas. The TAR-Down folding butt has an overall length of 900mm in the butt-open condition and 650mm in the butt-folding condition._
> 
> _5\. The rifle's versatility is further increased with the option to fit a 40x46mm UBGL GP-25, GP-30, and M6, catering to various operational requirements. Additionally, the inclusion of Tritium-filled sources for night firing and a Picatinny rail for mounting optical sights underlines the rifle’s adaptability to diverse scenarios._

  

In 2020, the Ordnance Factory of Tiruchirappalli (OFT) delivered the initial batch of 500 Trichy Assault Rifles (TAR) to the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF), fulfilling a total order of 6,167 assault rifles.

  

The procurement followed rigorous field trials, including evaluation sessions at the CRPF Academy in Kadarpur, Haryana, in November 2017. Testing focused on the TAR's functionality, accuracy, and reliability, with 15,000 rounds fired without a single stoppage, affirming the weapon's dependability.

  

OFT has further supplied over 10,000 rifles to Chhattisgarh police and various central armed reserve police forces, including the ITBP, BSF, and CISF. Shirish Khare, OFT's General Manager had proudly acclaimed the Trichy Assault Rifle as their most significant success in the past 12-13 years of weapons development.

  

With a focus on promoting indigenous weaponry, the adoption of the TAR by the BSF signifies an important step in fortifying the nation's Paramilitary security apparatus. This move aligns with broader initiatives to reduce dependence on foreign arms, fostering self-sufficiency in defence production.

2.content:
**Demand of TAR among Central Reserved Forces**

TAR or Trichy Assault Rifle is a product from erstwhile Ordinance Factory Trichy and now part of AWEIL. The development of the assault rifle was started in 2015 and a production line was established in 2017. The first batch of 200 TARs were delivered to Chandigarh police in March 2017. In November 2017, the CRPF tested the rifle’s functionality and its reliability. Over 15,000 rounds were fired to test the TAR’s life cycle and over 2,400 rounds to test its reliability. In February 2018, the TAR underwent field trial at Jagdalpur, Raipur, Guwahati and Srinagar. After regressive trials, the CRPF had placed an order for 6167 rifles TAR.

In January 2024, it was reported that BSF is acquiring 125 TAR rifles along with bayonets and other accessories. BSF has experience with operating TAR and has inducted the assault rifle into service earlier. Other Central Armed Police Forces which include SSB, ITBP & CISF has also procured TAR in some significant numbers. Police forces in several states have also inducted TAR under their modernisation scheme.

**TAR : Specifications**

The Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) is a 7.62X39mm powerful automatic weapon designed to destroy the enemy by fire in single and burst firing mode.  It has an effective range of 350m. Its light weight and modular design make it suitable for the counter-insurgency and counter-terror operations. It comes with foldable and fixed butt type, depending upon the requirement. The foldable butt version is helpful in quick and easy movement of personnel in guard and patrolling duty. The overall length of TAR-Down folding butt is 900mm in butt open condition and 650mm in butt folding condition. The rifle weighs 3.4kg and features a curved magazine with 30 rounds.

The rifle has mono-block receiver body & fibre reinforced polymer magazine with steel inserts. It also has a customised version with single round firing mode for police forces. It also features Tritium filled Sources for night firing and picatinny rail for mounting optical sights. It can also be fitted with Under barrel grenade launcher.

TAR very closely resembles Bulgarian Arsenal AR-M1F41. There is minor difference in the gas block & cleaning rod of the assault rifles. There is also some noticeable difference in the pistol grip. TAR is being supplied to paramilitary forces to reduce imports from Bulgaria. The unique feature of TAR is that it provides 12 O’clock rails on upper handguard which is not available in any other AKM copy. TAR is 7.62x39mm assault rifle, similar in calibre to AK-203. In fact TAR is almost equivalent to AK-103 and very close to AK-203 in terms of performance.

OFT hands over first batch of 500 Trichy Assault Rifles to CRPF

![Image 2: OFT hands over first batch of 500 Trichy Assault Rifles to CRPF](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-47529300,imgsize-110164,width-400,height-225,resizemode-72/47529300.jpg)

Trichy: The first batch of 500 Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) indigenously developed by the Ordnance Factory of Tiruchirappalli (OFT) was handed over to the Central Reserve Police Force (CRPF) at the factory premises on Thursday. The rifles are part of the total order for 6,167 rifles. OFT here has so far supplied around 11,000 TARs to various central and state police forces.

![Image 3: 1x1 polls](https://static.toiimg.com/photo/25581306.cms)

The rifles were received by CRPF DIG D S Rawat.  
Trichy Assault Rifle was conceived in 2015 and production began at OFT in 2017. TAR, is considered an equivalent variant of AK-47. Compared to stamped sheet metal riveted body in other rifles, TAR features a fully machined receiver body for higher reliability and strength.  
After Chhattisgarh state police received the first batch of 200 TARs in March 2017, various state police forces and paramilitary forces placed orders for the rifle. CRPF had conducted evaluation trials of TAR including accuracy and reliability apart from tests such as drop, mud, saltwater immersion and rain tests. The rifle was then subjected to life cycle test in which 15,000 rounds were fired without any single stoppage, proving its reliability. After successful trials, CRPF placed a pilot order for 100 rifles.  
After extensive field usage in various terrains including Srinagar, in 2018, CRPF placed the bulk order. CRPF had asked for customised requirements such as upper hand guard with picatinny rail for mounting telescopes and tritium filled luminous sources for night firing capability.  

“Our factory has produced several weapons. Among all, TAR is undoubtedly our biggest success,” said Shirish Khare, general manager, OFT.  
The ordnance factory here has 17,000 orders for TAR from Border Security Force and Sashastra Seema Bal.

![Image 2: Ordnance Factory launches new weapon ‘Trichy Carbine’](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-47529300,imgsize-110164,width-400,height-225,resizemode-72/47529300.jpg)

TRICHY: The Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli (OFT) on Thursday launched a new weapon called TriCa (Trichy Carbine), a mini version of the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR). The 7.62 X 39mm portable weapon launched on the carbine platform was entirely manufactured at the ordnance factory here.  
TriCa weighs 3.17kg (including the magazine) and is lighter compared to the assault rifles.

![Image 3: 1x1 polls](https://static.toiimg.com/photo/25581306.cms)

It is a compact automatic weapon designed for the crews of infantry combat vehicles, helicopters, paratroopers, state police force and special operation forces.  
OFT sources said that TriCa is equipped with a special muzzle booster to hide the flash and mitigate the sound during the firing. The weapon has an effective range of 150 to 175m. TriCa can use ammunition and magazines, as well as the interchangeable parts of general assault rifles (TAR and AK-47).  
The carbine can be hidden in the jackets of security personnel and even concealed under their clothes, an official said. The weapon was displayed during the defence exhibition held at Bengaluru a few months back. A source in the OFT said that several defence organisations and paramilitary units have expressed interest in the weapon. “Trichy Carbine best suits the CISF, state special police forces and NSG commandos. It will be easy to carry,” the source said.  
The field trials conducted yielded positive results. The weapon was launched by Sanjay Dwivedi, IOFS, general manager, OFT.

Trichy Assault Rifle with down-folding butt launched

![Image 2: Trichy Assault Rifle with down-folding butt launched](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-47529300,imgsize-110164,width-400,height-225,resizemode-72/47529300.jpg)

Trichy: Ordnance Factory of Tiruchirappalli (OFT) has introduced a variant of the indigenous Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) with a down-folding butt which has a destructive effect up to a range of 1,350m to commemorate the 75 years of Indian independence.  
OFT was so far manufacturing only two variants of TAR with a fixed butt and side-folding butt. Recently, the Central Armed Police Forces (CAPF) sought the factory to develop a down-folding butt variant for better portability in guarding and patrolling duty.

![Image 3: 1x1 polls](https://static.toiimg.com/photo/25581306.cms)

Some of the state police force and Railway Protection Force (RPF) also sought the new variant, OFT officials said.  
The total length of the 7.62X39mm TAR’s new down-folding butt variant is 900mm in open condition while it is 650mm in length in butt-folded condition. “We are prepared for the mass production of the new variant. The other variants were already well-received among various state police forces in the insurgence-prone areas including the red corridor,” a source with the OFT said.  
The automatic weapon TAR is designed to be engaged in single and burst firing mode. In burst mode, group or single targets at a range up to 500m can be destroyed, the OFT said.  
The new variant was launched by general manager of OFT, Sanjay Dwivedi.

'CRPF most likely to place orders for Trichy Assault Rifle'

[Deepak Karthik](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/toireporter/author-Deepak-Karthik-479250293.cms) / TNN / Updated: Mar 18, 2018, 11:34 IST

![Image 2: 'CRPF most likely to place orders for Trichy Assault Rifle'](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-63352432,imgsize-441613,width-400,height-225,resizemode-72/63352432.jpg)

Representative image

TRICHY: After Chhattisgarh, ample number of state police forces particularly from red corridor experiencing Naxalite-Maoist insurgency have placed orders for Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) besides the [Central Reserve Police Force](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/topic/central-reserve-police-force) ([CRPF](https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/topic/central-reserve-police-force)) that conducted field trials a few months back.  
Participating in the Ordnance Factories Day celebrated at the campus of Ordnance Factory of Tiruchirapalli (OFT) here on Saturday, Shirish Khare, General Manager of OFT said that the factory at present is developing two new weapons namely 7.62mm PKT (mountable) gun and 38mm Auto Grenade Launcher System (AGS).

![Image 3: 1x1 polls](https://static.toiimg.com/photo/25581306.cms)

  
The ordnance factory here established in 1966 by the then prime minister Indira Gandhi supplies rifle and grenade launchers to the Indian armed forces and paramilitary forces promoting the indigenous defence production. A year back, 7.62X39mm assault rifle christened as Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) available in both automatic and single fire modes was developed and launched by OFT to address the operational requirements of State police in red corridor (Maoist-Naxalite prone states).  
Initially, as Chhattisgarh state police alone had placed orders for procuring TAR, other state police forces have followed the suite which includes Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan, Kerala, and Mumbai police. Though Jharkhand has also shown interest in purchasing the indigenous weapon, OFT sources said that the state is yet to place orders. “Reception among the state police forces and Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) for TAR is exceptionally good. Even CRPF that conducted extensive field trials early in November 2017 is most likely to place the order,” Shirish Khare told TOI.

*   ##### Police to get modern assault rifles developed by Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli
    
    Telegraph | 2 December 2025
*   Kolkata Police are set to phase out their decades-old .303 guns and replace them with modern assault rifles developed by the Ordnance Factory Tiruchirappalli.The new Trichy Assault Rifles (TAR), modelled on the Bulgarian AR-M1 and described as an indigenous variant of the AK-47, are expected to arrive in batches early next year. “The consignment will reach in phases, and distribution will begin soon after,” an officer of the rank of deputy commissioner of Kolkata Police said.
    
    One of the biggest advantages is weight, senior officers said. The old .303 rifles weigh about 5.5kg, while the TAR is at least 2kg lighter.
    
    The officers said the rifle supports both single-shot and burst fire, allowing accurate engagement of targets up to 500 metres. “Its lightweight modular design and foldable butt make it handy, even for guard and patrolling duty,” a senior officer said.
    
    Kolkata Police have been phasing out ageing .303 rifles and replacing them with INSAS and SLRs (Self-Loading Rifles) in the force’s ongoing modernisation drive.
    
    But officers said the shift to TAR reflects the demands of contemporary policing, after the 26/11 Mumbai attack.
    
    “Several central forces, including the BSF and CRPF, have inducted TAR. This is currently the best option for our forces,” a senior officer said.
    
    The TAR has seen been used across the country. Chhattisgarh Police deployed the weapon during anti-Naxalite operations earlier this year, while Rajasthan, Jharkhand, and Madhya Pradesh police forces have also procured it, sources said. In addition to the TAR, Kolkata Police will procure around 200 automatic 9mm 1A pistols from Rifle Factory, Ishapore.
    
    “Non-lethal munitions from the Tear Smoke Unit in Tekanpur, Madhya Pradesh, are also on the upgrade list,” the officer said. Officers across units said such upgrades bolster not just capability but morale.
    
    “If one has to face a barrage of bullets from terrorists or armed criminals, modern firearms are essential. Personnel on the ground feel far more confident when they know they are equipped with the latest weapons,” a southeast division officer of Kolkata Police said.

Rising demand for Trichy assault rifle from red corridor: OFT GM

TNN / Updated: Mar 18, 2018, 11:17 IST

![Image 2: Rising demand for Trichy assault rifle from red corridor: OFT GM](https://static.toiimg.com/thumb/msid-63352237,imgsize-441613,width-400,height-225,resizemode-72/63352237.jpg)

Representative image

TRICHY: Ordnance Factory of Tiruchirapalli (OFT) general manager Shirish Khare has said that there is a rising demand for the Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR), from state police forces facing Naxal-Maoist insurgency in the country. Khare was speaking on the sidelines of Ordnance Factories Day on the OFT campus here on Saturday. He said that the factory was developing two new weapons - 7.62mm PKT (mountable) gun and 38mm auto grenade launcher system (AGS). A year ago, 7.62X39mm assault rifle christened as Trichy Assault Rifle (TAR) available in both automatic and single fire modes was developed and launched by OFT to address the operational requirements of the state police in red corridor (Maoist-Naxalite prone states).Initially, it was Chhattisgarh state police which had placed orders for procuring TAR. Considering the effectiveness of the weapon, the state police forces of Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Kerala as well as Mumbai police followed suit.Though Jharkhand has shown interest in purchasing the indigenous weapon, OFT sources said that the state is yet to place orders. “Reception among the state police forces and Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) for TAR is exceptionally good.

Even CRPF that conducted extensive field trials early in November 2017 is most likely to place the order,” Shirish Khare told TOI.The CRPF was said to have approved the indigenous weapon manufactured in OFT facility. TAR is an outcome of 1.5-year-old ‘7.62X39 mm Assault Rifle Project’ and is available in three variants such as fixed butt, side foldable, and under folding models.Official sources said that the OFT here has, thus far, supplied 1,200 units of TAR to state police forces, and in the next fiscal, as many as 1,700 units are expected to be supplied as part of fulfilling the total orders placed by police forces seeking 4,000 rifle units.“We are almost in the final stage of completing the new weapons such as PKT mountable gun and 38mm Auto Grenade Launcher System (AGS). Within a year, a prototype for those will be produced. So far, we have enough men and machinery to cater the needs. Modernisation is a periodical process,” Khare added.The OFT facility has an approximate workforce of 1,500 persons involved in manufacturing defence equipment. Meanwhile, the journey of OFT in developing small arms, modern weapons, and futuristic weapons was exhibited in photo and weapon exhibition on the OFT premises on Saturday for public view as a part of Ordnance Factories Day celebration.The ordnance factory established in 1966 by then prime minister Indira Gandhi supplies rifle and grenade launchers to the armed forces and paramilitary forces promoting the indigenous defence production.
